translations.text: If, then, beyond any doubt all these things must be left behind here, why do we not sell them and take their profit away with us?
But you, when you hand over gold and get a horse, are not grieved. Yet when you hand over these perishable things and the kingdom of heaven is given to you, do you weep over it?
You refuse the one who asks you. You do not want to give, and you gather countless excuses.
What will you answer the Judge? You who decorate walls, will you not clothe a human being?
You who cover horses with gold, do you ignore your brother who is shamefully naked? You who let wheat rot, will you not feed the hungry?
You who bury gold, if you see a debtor being choked by his creditor, will you treat him with contempt?
And if his wife is also found to be of the same mind, the disease is doubled. She multiplies luxuries, increases the love of fine tastes, and becomes a goad to desire.
They acquire stones of some kind, pearls, emeralds, jacinths and gold. Some of it they have hammered and some woven, and in every way they make that disease grow,
for they do not pursue these matters in passing. Night and day they are anxious about them.
And they gather craftsmen of every kind: they bring in dyers of brilliant dyes, goldsmiths, perfumers, weavers of gold, and painters.
They never have any rest, and no amount of wealth is enough to fulfil their desires, not even if it flowed up from a river,
when that foreign perfume is sought after as if it were ordinary oil from the market streets, and again those beautiful things that come out of the sea:
the murex shell and the pinna, more than sheep's wool. And gold is set around those costly stones:
some becomes a band for the forehead, some a necklace, other gold is spent on belts, other gold on the rings they put on their hands, and the rest on ornaments for the feet.
For these gold-lovers are glad to have their hands and feet bound, as long as gold is what binds them.
But when would such a man ever care for his own soul, when he is serving these evil desires of defilement?
For as a ship is wrecked by the violence of the waves and lost, so the desires of women sink those pitiable souls.
And when the wealth of these lovers of desire is spent like this on such things,
it never reaches the poor. Instead it is used up acquiring vain things.
And if he hears, "Sell your possessions and give to the poor, so that you may have provisions for the journey to eternal life," he goes away grieved.
But if he hears, "Give money for the women, to singers, or give it to stonecutters, goldsmiths, carpenters,
gold-embroiderers and painters," he is glad, as though something precious and better than money were being given to him.
O man, do you not see these walls, ruined by the passing of time? Only parts of them are left in the city, and they lie there only to trip up people walking by.
How many poor people must there have been in this city when these walls were being put up? The rich ignored them because they were so eager to build.
So where now is their brilliant decoration? Or where is the man who was envied for building them?
